top.title: Twisted Path Distillery will leave the Lincoln Warehouse at year's end and move to San Diego
top.dek: After 13 years in Milwaukee, the organic distillery pours its last Bay View drinks Dec. 31.
top.body:
Twisted Path Distillery, the organic spirits maker and cocktail bar in the Lincoln Warehouse at 2018 S. 1st St., will close its Milwaukee operation on Dec. 31 and reopen in San Diego early next year, OnMilwaukee reported Thursday.

Owners Brian Sammons and Laura Singleton moved to Southern California a while ago to be near family, and Sammons has been commuting back to run the still. He told the outlet that managing a distillery from that far away was "exactly as hard as it sounds."

Before it goes, the distillery plans a 13th-anniversary party on Saturday, Dec. 5, to release a 12-year single-barrel rye that it says is the oldest Wisconsin-grain rye made and aged in the state. The owners say they want December to feel like a send-off celebration, so expect a busy tasting room through the holidays.

image.alt: The red-brick Twisted Path Distillery tasting room at the base of the Lincoln Warehouse on S. 1st Street at dusk

safety.title: Police oversight board holds off on recommending an end to Milwaukee's license plate cameras
safety.dek: After nearly two hours of debate, the Fire and Police Commission tabled a proposed ban on plate readers like Flock.
safety.body:
Milwaukee's Fire and Police Commission on Thursday night delayed a vote on a resolution urging the Police Department to stop using automatic license plate readers, including the Flock cameras mounted on poles around the city, WISN reported.

Commission Vice Chair Krissie Fung, who brought the proposal, questioned whether the cameras' crime-solving benefits outweigh privacy risks, while Commissioner Ruben Burgos argued the technology works and the city could switch vendors instead. Commissioners pressed police on what data is stored and who can see it, including outside companies and federal agencies, and dozens of residents spoke in favor of a ban.

The vote to hold the resolution means it could return in amended form, but no date has been set. Police told WISN in October that they planned to renew the Flock contract soon.

image.alt: A solar-powered license plate reader camera mounted on a metal light pole among trees

help.title: Families with Anthem coverage could lose in-network care at Children's Wisconsin on Jan. 1
help.dek: The hospital and insurer remain at an impasse with their contract set to expire Dec. 31.
help.body:
Children's Wisconsin and Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield have not reached a new contract, and the current one runs out Dec. 31, CBS 58 reported Thursday. Without a deal, thousands of children covered by Anthem could find the hospital and its clinics out of network starting Jan. 1.

Families began receiving notices this week through the Children's patient portal. Parents of kids with ongoing specialty care told the station they have few alternatives in the region.

If your family has Anthem, it's worth checking your plan's continuity-of-care options now and asking your child's care team about upcoming appointments before the deadline.

image.alt: The Children's Wisconsin hospital tower in Wauwatosa on a sunny fall day

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Burnhearts
spotlight.dek: A Logan Avenue tavern with a long past, an aged-beer stash and the February block party that fills the street
spotlight.body:
Burnhearts is a dimly lit corner tavern at 2599 S. Logan Ave., a few blocks east of Kinnickinnic Avenue on a mostly residential stretch of Bay View. It is a beer bar first: when Urban Milwaukee visited in 2013 it counted 24 taps and two casks, and the bar's website still keeps separate draft, bottle-and-can and cocktail lists.

William "B.J." Seidel and Jess Seidel bought the building in October 2006, spent about eight months renovating it and opened on June 8, 2007. The name honors William's great-grandmother. The corner has poured drinks for a long time. Before Burnhearts it was Carl's, a mid-century supper club, then Suds, O'Brien's Call Box and Flanigan's Call Box. Neighborhood lore says it was a brothel and gambling parlor during Prohibition, a story Urban Milwaukee warned might be embellished. A 2016 Bar Exam column traced the tavern to the 1890s or earlier.

Regulars come for the beer. William Seidel ages imperial stouts, barley wines and sours in a walk-in cooler and releases them on a list called Carl's Private Stash, named after the old supper club. Brandy has a following too. The draft list on the bar's website includes Central Waters' barrel-aged Brandyland Old Fashioned. In July 2018 the Seidels opened a back patio, a project they had planned since about a year after opening and set aside during the recession. It has a gate built by JR's Welding & Fabrication and a floral mural by bartender Mic Makalinao.

The bar is best known around town for Mitten Fest, a February block party on the street outside the tavern, which it has run since 2013 for Hunger Task Force. Milwaukee Magazine reported that it drew nearly 10,000 people. When COVID-19 canceled the 2021 party, the bar sold bottled cocktails to go on Sundays as "Miss You Fest" and gave part of the proceeds to the food bank. For 2024 the owners passed the party to Boone & Crockett so they could take a year to "re-envision" their own space. It came back to Logan Avenue on Feb. 7, 2026, with The Hallelujah Ward headlining. Each summer the bar also hosts the Burnhearts/Pabst Street Party, which has run for more than a decade.

Burnhearts' own Instagram has been quiet since a late-October post, and it hasn't announced anything for this week. Its back room still draws music, though: in late August, people who were there posted photos and video of a set by Promise Ring singer Davey von Bohlen. Watch @burnhearts this winter for the next Mitten Fest date and lineup.

Burnhearts, 2599 S. Logan Ave. Open Mon.–Fri. 3 pm–2 am and Sat.–Sun. noon–2 am, per its website. burnheartsbar.com · @burnhearts on Instagram

history.title: Three Brothers: the Schlitz saloon that became a Serbian landmark
history.text: In 1897 Schlitz built a turreted tavern on St. Clair Street. Six decades later a Serbian family turned it into Three Brothers, still serving today.
history.body:
The little cream city brick building at 2414 S. St. Clair St. began as a beer outlet, not a restaurant. In July 1897 the Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company bought the small triangular lot from a local couple for $250, and on July 26 it applied for a permit to build a tavern there. Milwaukee architect Charles Kirchhoff, who drew plans for several Schlitz taverns around the city, designed it in the Queen Anne style, at an estimated cost of $5,000.

It was a "tied house": the brewery owned the building and leased it to an operator who could pour only Schlitz. The giveaway is still on the roof, where a corner turret is topped by a belted globe, the brewery's trademark. Around 1920, when breweries were pushed to sell off property unrelated to making beer, most tied houses like this one passed to private owners.

The building's second life began in the 1950s. Milun Radicevic, a Serbian veteran of World War II who came to Milwaukee in 1949, had been running a tavern on South 2nd Street since 1953. He moved the business to St. Clair Street and named it Three Brothers for his three sons. His wife, Milunka, created the original menu of Serbian home cooking, much of it made from scratch. The family and its website date the move to 1956; the 1976 National Register nomination says the owners bought the building in 1958.

Recognition followed. The city named the tavern a Milwaukee landmark in 1976, and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 11, 1977, as the Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company Saloon. In 2002 Three Brothers won a James Beard Foundation America's Classics award. A granddaughter told OnMilwaukee the place was "our family's Ellis Island."

Nearly 130 years after Schlitz built it, the turret and globe still mark the corner, and the third generation of the family still runs the restaurant.

image.alt: Black-and-white 1976 photo of the cream brick corner tavern at 2414 S. St. Clair St., with a conical turret topped by the belted Schlitz globe and 'Three Brothers Tavern' signs in the windows
image.credit: Paul S. Pagel, Milwaukee Landmarks Commission, 1976 / National Register of Historic Places nomination, National Park Service

weekend.intro: The holiday season starts creeping into Bay View this weekend, with a small-business block party on Delaware Avenue and chai nog back on the menu at Twisted Path. In between there's a full slate of all-ages shows, a free library conversation and a couple of good causes.

picks.title: The Frozen Chair Market
picks.why: Saturday's small-business block party with Component Brewing is a chance to start holiday shopping close to home.

picks.title: Humbird, Bad Posture Club + Chris Rosenau
picks.why: Milwaukee Record's pick for Saturday: Humbird brings songs from its fourth album to an all-ages Cactus Club show, $10 in advance.

picks.title: Death Café
picks.why: A free, unhurried Saturday-afternoon conversation at the library about life, death and everything in between.

picks.title: DIY Beaded Necklace Workshop
picks.why: An all-ages Sunday drop-in where kids and adults can string a necklace together from a big bead collection.

picks.title: Clementine’s bowling fundraiser for homeless vets
picks.why: Bowl a few frames at Bay View Bowl on Sunday and the profits go to the Milwaukee Homeless Veterans Initiative.

briefing.text: Foggy start, then partly sunny and mild, with a high near 63.
Twisted Path Distillery will close its Lincoln Warehouse tasting room Dec. 31 and move to San Diego.
Today: Yr Knives and Book of Johns play an in-store show at Acme Records, 8:30 pm.
Buzz: a neighbor's free cookbook giveaway at Pine and Wilbur lost a whole box to one taker.
Spotlight: Burnhearts, the Logan Avenue tavern behind Mitten Fest.
